summary: Passport eaten by a giraffe at breakfast
story: On the morning of July 1 I was having breakfast at Twiga House in Nairobi, where the resident giraffes put their heads through the dining room windows. My passport was on the table next to my plate because the front desk had just handed it back to me. A giraffe called Daisy took it off the table and ate most of it before anyone could get it back. What I recovered was the cover and part of page 3. The lodge manager has written a letter confirming this. He was very apologetic, although he did mention that Daisy had never done it before. I went to the US Embassy in Nairobi the next day for an emergency passport. I am claiming the passport fee, the photos and the taxis to and from the embassy.

The hotel drove me to a clinic, where a doctor examined me, took an X-ray of the shoulder and prescribed painkillers. Nothing was broken. I am claiming the clinic bill and the pharmacy bill. The county has declared the house uninhabitable and I am staying with my aunt and uncle, so on June 16 I canceled the trip I had booked to Seattle for June 20. I had been looking forward to seeing the Emerald City. For now I have come to the view that there is no place like home, once we have one again. summary: Valise stolen from a train at the Gare de Lyon

At the Gare de Lyon I put my valise on the luggage rack in our carriage and stepped off the train to buy a bottle of water for the journey. I was gone for perhaps ten minutes. When I came back the valise was gone. It held my clothes and, far worse, all of my husband's writing: the printed manuscript of his novel, his notebooks and the backup drive, which I had packed so that he could work on everything in Switzerland. There are no other copies. I reported it to the police at the station that afternoon. I have valued the manuscript and notebooks at $1,900, though my husband would call that figure an insult.

summary: Hospital admission in Mexico City with a kidney stone
story: On July 22, two days into my trip to Mexico City, I had terrible pain in my left side at the hotel. It came out of nowhere. I took a taxi to a private hospital, where they found a kidney stone causing a blockage and kept me for two nights. They removed the stone the next day. I paid $6,200 by card when I was discharged. I was told that the altitude and not drinking enough water on the flight may have played a part. The hospital's discharge summary and the bill are attached.

items.description: Two night hospital admission, CT scan and kidney stone removal

documents.name: Hospital discharge summary
documents.content:
HOSPITAL ANGELES DEL VALLE, MEXICO CITY. DEPARTMENT OF UROLOGY. DISCHARGE SUMMARY.

Patient: Robert Haines. Date of birth: February 3, 1965. Age: 61. Nationality: United States. Admitted: July 22, 2026 at 21:40 through the emergency department. Discharged: July 24, 2026 at 11:15. Attending physician: Dr. Luis Ortega Marin, Urology.

REASON FOR ADMISSION. Severe pain in the left flank radiating to the groin, of sudden onset at the patient's hotel at approximately 19:30, with nausea and two episodes of vomiting. The patient arrived by taxi and was unable to sit still during the assessment.

FINDINGS ON ARRIVAL. Blood pressure 152/90. Heart rate 102, regular. Temperature 37.1 C. Oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air, consistent with the altitude of Mexico City. Marked tenderness over the left flank. Abdomen soft, no guarding. No fever and no signs of sepsis.

INVESTIGATIONS. Urinalysis: blood 3+, no nitrites, no leukocytes. Complete blood count normal. Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, mildly raised. Electrolytes normal. C-reactive protein normal. Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis on July 22: a 6 mm stone in the upper left ureter with moderate hydronephrosis of the left kidney. No stones in the right kidney. No other acute findings.

HISTORY OBTAINED FROM THE PATIENT. The patient reports high blood pressure treated with lisinopril. He passed a kidney stone without treatment in 2022 and has taken potassium citrate since then. On direct questioning he describes an episode of left flank pain with visible blood in the urine in the spring of this year. He reports that he saw his urologist at home about it on May 14, 2026, that a CT scan at that visit showed a 5 mm stone in the lower part of the left kidney, that his potassium citrate was increased from 10 mEq to 20 mEq twice daily and tamsulosin was added, and that he was advised to return for repeat imaging in August, which he had not yet done. He reports that the pain settled within a few days in May, that he considered the matter dealt with and that he did not think to mention it when arranging his travel. He takes no other regular medication. No known drug allergies.

DIAGNOSIS. Obstructing stone of the left ureter with hydronephrosis. In the opinion of the treating team this is the stone documented in the left kidney in May 2026, which has since moved into the ureter. Reduced fluid intake during travel and the dry air at the altitude of Mexico City, approximately 2,240 meters, may have contributed to the timing of the episode.

TREATMENT IN HOSPITAL. Admitted to the urology ward. Treated with intravenous fluids, ketorolac and morphine for pain, and ondansetron for nausea. The pain did not settle overnight and kidney function did not improve, so the patient was taken to the operating room on July 23. Procedure: left ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation of the stone and placement of a ureteral stent, under general anesthesia. The stone was cleared completely. No complications. Fragments were sent for analysis and the result will follow by email.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE. Comfortable, eating and drinking normally, passing urine without difficulty. Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL on the morning of discharge. Mild discomfort from the stent, as expected.

MEDICATION AT DISCHARGE. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily while the stent is in place. Potassium citrate 20 mEq twice daily, continued. Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for stent discomfort. Lisinopril continued.

ADVICE AND FOLLOW UP. The patient should drink at least 2.5 liters of water a day. He is fit to fly home as planned. The ureteral stent must be removed by his urologist within two weeks, and he has been given a letter and the operative note to take with him. He should go to an emergency department if he develops a fever, cannot pass urine or has pain that does not respond to medication.

Signed: Dr. Luis Ortega Marin, Urology. July 24, 2026.

summary: Prescription sunglasses stolen by a monkey at Uluwatu Temple
story: On August 19 I visited Uluwatu Temple in Bali. A macaque jumped onto my shoulder from a wall, stole my prescription sunglasses off my face and ran to the cliff edge with them. Our guide tried to trade for them, which he says usually works. The monkey turned down a banana and then a bag of peanuts, and in the end it dropped my sunglasses over the cliff. I asked at the police post by the temple gate about reporting the theft, and the officer smiled and said they do not take reports about the monkeys. So I asked our guide to write a letter instead, which is attached. I need prescription lenses to drive, so I had a replacement pair made in Denpasar the next day for $240.

summary: Thirty hour delay on the sleeper train from Istanbul to Paris
story: I was traveling from Istanbul to Paris in the Calais coach of the Simplon Express. At Belgrade on July 20 we were told that floods had washed out the line between Vinkovci and Brod, and we were held for thirty hours. The dining car ran out of nearly everything on the first day, so I bought my meals for cash from the station buffet and from a woman selling pastries on the platform, about $140 in all, and nobody gave receipts. I also paid to rebook my connection in Paris. I should add that the delay was made longer by an incident in the compartment next to mine, which a Belgian gentleman with a remarkable mustache insisted on resolving before any of us could leave the dining car. I had told the conductor there was a man in my compartment. Nobody listens.

summary: Nine hour delay leaving Dallas for Vancouver
story: Our flight from Dallas to Vancouver on July 3 was due out at 8:15 in the morning and left at 5:32 in the afternoon. After we had boarded, the captain told us there was a fault with a fuel pump and that a part was coming from Houston, and they took us back off the plane. We had breakfast and lunch in the terminal while we waited. I asked Northwind for a letter for my insurance and they sent the delay certificate that is attached, with the meal receipts. I am claiming $61 for the two of us.

summary: Phone snatched from her hand in La Candelaria
story: On July 8 I was walking in La Candelaria in Bogota, checking a map on my phone, when a man ran past and took the phone out of my hand. I went to the police the same afternoon and their report is attached, along with the receipt for the phone, which I bought in March. I sent this in from my hostel in July but I am not sure it went through, so I am filing it again now that I am home.

summary: Fourteen hour delay leaving Anchorage for Las Vegas
story: My flight home from Anchorage on August 9 was due out at 11:55 in the morning and left at 2:10 the next morning. The gate agent announced that the first officer had run out of duty hours and that a replacement was being flown up from Seattle. I had lunch and dinner in the terminal, which has one restaurant and a stuffed bear, and I ate both meals facing the bear. Skylark sent me the attached certificate when I asked for one for my insurance. I am claiming $71 for the two meals.
